events.description: Revolution of April 27-28, 1978 brought the Democratic Republic of Afghanistan (DRA) to power.
Ambassador Eliot's cable, 'Six Weeks after Afghanistan's Revolution: A Summing Up', sent to the State Department.
Revolution in Afghanistan (April 27-28) brought the DRA to power, ending Daoud's rule.
US Embassy Kabul cable summarizing the situation six weeks after the revolution and recommending that the US shore up Iran and Pakistan against the Soviet-backed regime.
A nationwide nighttime curfew remains in effect and DRA security arrangements are strict.

relationships.detail: The DRA relies completely on the USSR for military supplies and increasingly for economic assistance.
relationships.quote: RELIES ON HUNDRED PERCENT ON THE SOVIET UNION FOR MILITARY SUPPLIES AND EQUIPMENT, AND INCREASINGLY ON THE SOVIET UNION FOR ECONOMIC ASSISTANCE

relationships.detail: Ambassador at Kabul, sender of the cable.
DRA leaders are ideologically inspired by the USSR and follow its model.
relationships.quote: THE LEADERS OF THE DRA HAVE BEEN IDEOLOGICALLY INSPIRED BY THE SOVIET UNION

relationships.detail: The DRA is described as overwhelmingly dependent on the Soviet Union and relying on it entirely for military supplies and increasingly for economic aid.
relationships.quote: RELIES ON HUNDRED PERCENT ON THE SOVIET UNION FOR MILITARY SUPPLIES AND EQUIPMENT, AND INCREASINGLY ON THE SOVIET UNION FOR ECONOMIC ASSISTANCE

relationships.detail: The DRA is the new government of Afghanistan following the April 1978 revolution.
relationships.quote: THE NEW GOVERNMENT OF THE DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF AFGHANISTAN (DRA)

relationships.detail: The DRA took power through the April 1978 revolution that ousted the Daoud regime.
relationships.quote: WHY THE SOVIET UNION WANTS TO DOMINATE AFGHANISTAN... YOUNG LEADERS... DAOUD

relationships.detail: The ambassador says the Soviets had already obtained their strategic and economic goals in Afghanistan under Daoud.
relationships.quote: SOVIETS GOT WHAT THEY WANTED OUT OF AFGHANISTAN STRATEGICALLY AND ECONOMICALLY

relationships.detail: The ambassador expects DRA foreign policy toward Pakistan to be heavily influenced by Soviet wishes and thinks the DRA may keep the Pushtunistan and Baluchistan cards available for future use.
relationships.quote: ITS FOREIGN POLICY, PARTICULARLY TOWARD PAKISTAN AND IRAN, IS LIKELY TO BE HEAVILY INFLUENCED BY THE WISHES OF THE SOVIET UNION

relationships.detail: DRA policy toward Iran is expected to follow Soviet wishes, and Iran is described as threatened by the Soviet-backed regime in Afghanistan.
relationships.quote: AGAINST THE NEW THREAT TO THEIR SECURITY POSED BY THE SOVIET-BACKED REGIME IN AFGHANISTAN

key_claims: The DRA is overwhelmingly dependent on the Soviet Union and cannot stay in power without Soviet help.
The DRA represents a minority of Afghans, and the middle class, clergy and tribes oppose it, but this opposition is fragmented and leaderless.
A more likely scenario than a coup is assassinations, terrorism and guerrilla warfare in the tribal areas adjoining Pakistan.
The Soviet embrace of the DRA is tight, and Afghan independence from Moscow is doubtful.
The Soviets are expected to repay their aid with Afghan minerals such as gas, petroleum and copper.
The U.S. should keep an adequate presence in Afghanistan and shore up Iran and Pakistan against the Soviet-backed regime.
